title: Nuclear Power in the Energy Transition: A Multidimensional Framework for Electricity and Thermal Energy Applications
content: The ongoing debate on nuclear power calls for a broader assessment of its potential role in the energy transition, extending beyond its established application in electricity generation. This paper provides a quantitative and multidimensional analysis of nuclear energy, bringing together historical data, technological performance indicators, energy consumption patterns and information on current and potential applications. Although nuclear power currently accounts for approximately 9% of global electricity generation, electricity itself represents only about 21% of final energy consumption. This highlights the importance of examining the potential contribution of nuclear energy to thermal applications, particularly since the use of nuclear heat for non-electric purposes remains very limited, amounting to less than 3 TWh worldwide. Attention is therefore given to cogeneration, industrial heat applications and hydrogen production. Although electrification will play a central role in decarbonisation, several energy services may remain difficult to electrify directly, making the availability of low-carbon thermal energy an important aspect of future energy systems. The paper analyses the technological characteristics and limitations of nuclear power, distinguishing between established applications and potential developments, and discusses the conditions required for its effective integration into different energy-system contexts. Four key dimensions are identified: energy-system requirements, technological and industrial capabilities, regulatory and institutional conditions, and economic and financial factors. A preliminary multi-criteria assessment framework is proposed to support the evaluation of alternative nuclear development pathways and their potential contribution to the energy transition.
